title: Visual annotation basics
description: Marking up a captured observation, associating a mark with a target on purpose, and saving immutable annotation evidence.

steps.narration: This is the Observer viewer, running locally against a project that has already captured one observation. Everything you are about to see is read from evidence on disk. The viewer never re-opens the inspected page to fill in a gap.

The observation is listed under the human alias its project gave it, baseline, rather than under a generated identifier. An alias is how a person refers to evidence; the identifier underneath it stays the machine's business.

callout.text: Captured evidence, selected by its human alias.

steps.narration: Observer derives the geometric relationships between targets and can draw them over the screenshot. They are switched off here so the annotation work stays readable. Turning a view off changes nothing about the evidence underneath.

The toolbar has separate modes, and that separation is deliberate. One pointer drag could plausibly mean draw a shape, move a shape, or pan the canvas. Rather than guess from context, the viewer makes you say which one you meant.

callout.text: Select, Pan and the drawing modes are separate so a drag is never ambiguous.

steps.narration: Pan mode moves your view of the screenshot without touching anything in it. Navigating evidence and editing evidence are different activities, so they get different modes.
Now to the marks themselves. A point simply says: look here. It is the smallest thing you can record.
Placing it on the first card records a position in the screenshot's own coordinates. Notice what has not happened: nothing has been said about the card, and nothing has been asked of anyone.
A rectangle covers an area rather than a position, which is the usual way to talk about a whole region of the page.
Dragging one across the hero banner records exactly that area. The rectangle happens to sit over the hero, but the viewer has not concluded anything from that overlap, and it will not.
A line records a span between two places, which is how people usually point at a distance or an edge.
This one runs across the call-to-action band.
An arrow is a line that also points. It is worth being precise about what that means here.

This one runs from the first card toward the second, pointing right. That is a fact about the drawing, not an instruction about the layout. The viewer records the geometry and stops there. If you want the arrow to mean move this to the right, you will have to say so yourself, which the next tutorial covers.

callout.text: A drawn direction is evidence of what you drew, not a decision about the page.

steps.narration: A note carries words. The text is written first, so that placing the note is a single deliberate act rather than an empty marker you have to remember to fill in later.

action.value: Illustration feels crowded against the caption

steps.narration: Switching to Note mode.
The note is anchored beside the illustration. Five marks now exist, and every one of them is still only a record of something a person noticed.
Back in Select mode the marks become things you can pick up and inspect, instead of strokes you are laying down.
Selecting the rectangle that was drawn over the hero shows what Observer actually believes about it.

No association. The rectangle covers the hero on screen, yet Observer refuses to claim the mark is about the hero. Overlap is genuinely ambiguous: you might mean the region, the thing next to it, the gap between them, or the whole area. Guessing would turn your drawing into a claim you never made.

callout.text: Drawing over a target does not associate it. Overlap is not meaning.

steps.narration: So the association is made explicitly. First the hero target is chosen from the configured targets this observation captured.
Then the mark is bound to it. Now the record says this rectangle is about the hero, because a person said so, not because two shapes happened to overlap.
Saving writes this set of marks to disk as one immutable annotation artifact, tied to the exact observation it was drawn on. From here it is evidence with provenance, not a sketch in a browser tab.
The annotation now appears in the saved list for this observation, which is what proves it survived the round trip to disk rather than merely looking saved.
Reloading the viewer from scratch proves the point. Nothing is being remembered in the page.
Reopening the same observation brings the saved annotation back from disk, exactly as it was written.
Opening the saved annotation loads its marks for editing. What happens next is the part worth understanding.

The draft is labelled a revision, not an edit. Saving again will write a new annotation that records which one it revises, and the original stays on disk untouched. Evidence accumulates; it is never quietly rewritten, because the history of what someone thought is often the most useful part of the record.

callout.text: Editing produces a revision. The earlier annotation is never overwritten.
